newsitem.title: GERMANY: Chartists say Germany's DAX bulls down, but not out.
newsitem.headline: Chartists say Germany's DAX bulls down, but not out.

text.p: German stock market bulls are down but not out as technical signals point to a rising market again in six to eight weeks after the current consolidation ends, chartists said on Monday.

At one point during the recent correction, the DAX index was nearly 10 percent off its record high of 3,475.18 points in electronic trade, and dealers bemoaned the sudden end of the greatest bull run in German history.

But the DAX index of German blue chips staged a dramatic recovery on Monday, ending bourse trade up 67.95 points, or 2.09 percent, at 3,312.88 points. The IBIS index measuring electronic trade later closed up 3.32 percent at 3,342.77 points.
The market last week reacted to a mixed set of fundamental factors, most importantly a small increase in U.S. short-term interest rates, by following the Dow Jones index sharply lower.
Clear market signals from fundamental factors were hard to find, but technical analysts remained upbeat for the short-to-medium term outlook, predicting that the DAX could test the 3,500 level.

"A key question is whether the gap that we saw last week can be filled and whether the market can break through extremely strong resistance at 3,330 points," said Wieland Staud, chief strategist in German equities at Yamaichi Bank.
"If this decisive points of resistance is broken, then it is likely that the index will rise very quickly to around 3,410 points," Staud said.
"I see the recent fall as an interruption to the bull market, which could last six or eight weeks. But it does not mean the end of the bull market altogether," said Staud.

Marcel Mussler, chartist at DG Bank in Frankfurt, also remains in bullish mode. "The target area for the DAX to hit during the correction was between 3,160 points and 3,220 points and this 60-point area was clearly and swiftly reached," said Mussler.
"What is also helpful is the U.S. dollar, which has consolidated and now is giving new buy signals and this is the fuel for a rise in shares," said Mussler.
"We see a sideways range of between 3,150 and 3,600 points until the late summer and our target is still for 3,500/3,600 points by year-end," he said.

"In terms of sectors, we are positive on engineering stocks, cars and chemicals are also coming again. Relative performance in the chemical sector is heading upwards again after a four-month break," said Mussler.
Giro Olbertz, chartist at Vereins und West Bank in Hamburg, remains bullish in the short-term but is forecasting a more serious correction in coming months.
"I would tend to view the coming weeks positively for the market and am looking at another attempt on the 3,500-point level on the DAX," said Olbertz.
"The reason is the way support for the DAX has held at between 3,200 and 3,250 points, even if it fell below 3,200 on an intraday basis," he said.
"I reckon that the DAX index will rise to around 3,500 points in the short-term and thereafter that we will see a bigger fall within the next four weeks," said Olbertz.
The fall after the market hit the 3,500 point level would be bigger than the recent 10 percent slide, Olbertz said.
He sees a level by the end of the year below that of last year's closing rate or even lower at 2,880 points, where support would be strong.

Heaviest hit by this fall would be the big chemical stocks, as the cycle of overperformance by these stocks was over, Olbertz said, while the construction sector was set to report an disproportionately strong performance.
